entries.title: Tell me about yourself, in two minutes
entries.summary: The question most interviews open with: a simple order for the answer, and what to leave out.

parts.text: Start with now: what you do today (your role, or your course and year) and the one thing you do best in it, in one or two sentences.
Then the past: one or two experiences that led here, each with a result you can name, such as a report you built, a process you sped up or a project you shipped.
Then next: the role you are applying for and why this team. Read the job description first and use its words where they are true for you.
Keep it near two minutes, about 250 to 300 spoken words. Say it out loud a few times, but don't learn it word for word.
Leave out your date of birth, family details and salary. The question is about your work, and those come up later, if at all.

entries.title: Answering "Tell me about a time when…" with STAR
entries.summary: Situation, Task, Action, Result: a way to give a story answer that stays short and ends with what changed.

parts.text: Situation: one or two sentences of background, enough for a stranger to follow. Where you were, and what was going on.
Task: what you had to do, or the problem you owned. Keep it to your part, not the whole team's.
Action: most of the answer. The steps you took yourself, in order. Say "I", not "we", for the parts you did.
Result: what changed, with a number if you have one (time saved, errors fixed, users reached), and what you would do differently next time.
Keep three or four stories ready that you can bend to many questions: a deadline, a mistake you fixed, a disagreement, something you learned fast.

entries.title: SQL drills on one orders table
entries.summary: Six queries on a table orders(order_id, customer_id, order_date, amount, status), each with the answer explained.

parts.text: Count the orders whose status is 'delivered'.
parts.answer: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered'; WHERE keeps only the matching rows before they are counted.

parts.text: Show each customer's total amount, biggest first.
parts.answer: SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY total DESC; Every column in the list is either grouped or inside an aggregate.

parts.text: List the customers with more than 3 orders.
parts.answer: SELECT customer_id FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 3; WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters the groups after it.

parts.text: Show each customer's first order date.
parts.answer: SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date) AS first_order FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id; MIN works on dates as well as numbers.

parts.text: Find the orders with no amount recorded.
parts.answer: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE amount IS NULL; amount = NULL is never true, so it returns nothing. Use IS NULL.

parts.text: Number each customer's orders from newest to oldest.
parts.answer: SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) AS n FROM orders; PARTITION BY restarts the count for each customer, and unlike GROUP BY it keeps every row.

entries.title: Windows sign-in and process events
entries.summary: Six Windows Security log events a SOC analyst reads every day, and what each one can point to.

parts.text: Which event ID records a failed sign-in?
parts.answer: 4625. Many of them for one account from one source in a few minutes usually means someone is guessing passwords.

parts.text: Which event ID records a successful sign-in, and what tells you how the person signed in?
parts.answer: 4624. Its logon type does: 2 is at the keyboard, 3 is over the network, 10 is Remote Desktop.

parts.text: A 4625 burst is followed by a 4624 for the same account from the same address. What do you check first?
parts.answer: Whether the guessing worked: what that session did next (processes started, files touched) and whether the sign-in was expected for that user and place.

parts.text: Which event ID records a new process, and what must be on for it to appear?
parts.answer: 4688. Process creation auditing has to be turned on; to see the full command line, the command-line setting must be on too.

parts.text: Which event ID records a new user account being created?
parts.answer: 4720. An account made outside the normal joining process, or late at night, is worth a look.

parts.text: The Security log shows event 1102. Why does it matter?
parts.answer: 1102 means the audit log was cleared. Attackers clear logs to hide what they did, so it usually calls for escalation.
